Woe

/woh/ — rhymes with know · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Woe is a strong feeling of sadness or distress.

The farmer's tale of woe included a flood, a drought, and a broken tractor all in one year.

Worked Example

A small business owner describes her past year: supply chain failures left her warehouse empty, a key employee quit unexpectedly, and a data breach cost her thousands. She calls it her 'year of woe.'

The situation isn't a single sad event—it's a cascade of troubles all hitting together. 'Woe' is more precise than plain 'sadness' because it captures that compounded, stacked-up suffering, as if telling a story of disasters. Sadness alone doesn't convey that narrative weight.

How Woe Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

sadness

sadness: the plain, everyday feeling of unhappiness

sorrow

sorrow: deep sadness, often over a loss

anguish

anguish: sharp, almost unbearable emotional pain

Antonyms

joy

joy: bright, uncomplicated happiness and delight

bliss

bliss: a state of perfect, untroubled happiness

How Strong Is It? — sadness → sorrow → anguish → woe

sadness vs. woe

sadness vs. woe: Sadness is much weaker than woe — sadness is one gloomy afternoon, while woe piles trouble upon trouble into a whole tale of misery.

sorrow vs. woe

sorrow vs. woe: Sorrow is deeper than plain sadness but still weaker than woe; sorrow grieves a single loss, while woe suggests a string of misfortunes weighing someone down.

anguish vs. woe

anguish vs. woe: Anguish comes close to woe in intensity, but woe is the stronger, more sweeping term — anguish is one moment of searing pain, while woe names deep distress that colors someone's whole situation.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — wā

Root — wā: a cry of grief; misery, wretchedness (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Woe began as the Old English wail of grief itself — 'wā!' — so the word literally is the cry of misery, which is why it names deep sadness and a pile-up of troubles.

Use the root in a new word: woeful

Use the root in a new word: woeful: The team gave a woeful performance, so full of errors that the fans trudged home carrying a little of the players' woe themselves.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal / literary

Woe is grand and serious—the sadness of kings or a tragic hero. Reach for it when troubles pile up and the suffering is deep and ongoing. For everyday unhappiness, 'sadness' is simpler and better.
